title: Conservative Q-learning: objectives, derivations and value bounds
description: From offline Bellman error to the CQL objective: entropy duality, policy-value lower bounds, and continuous-action importance sampling.
body:
These notes follow the conservative Q-learning objective from its tabular update to the loss used in a continuous-action critic. The distinction between a lower bound on every action value and a lower bound on a policy's expected value matters throughout the derivation. Notation and the source of the error Let $d_{\mathcal D}(s)$ denote the dataset's state marginal and let $\beta(a|s)=\hat\pi_\beta(a|s)$ denote its empirical action probabilities. In the tabular calculations below, assume $d_{\mathcal D}(s)>0$ and $\beta(a|s)>0$ for each state-action pair being analyzed. This is an analysis assumption, not a description of sparse continuous-action data. For a fixed policy $\pi$, its Bellman operator is $$
(\mathcal B^\pi Q)(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'|s,a)\sum_{a'}\pi(a'|s')Q(s',a').
$$ The dataset can constrain the left-hand side only at observed actions. The expectation on the right can still evaluate poorly supported actions. A small training TD error therefore does not establish that the policy's value estimate is accurate outside the dataset. For example, suppose the true values of two actions are $Q^\pi(s,a_1)=1$ and $Q^\pi(s,a_2)=0$, but the dataset contains only $a_1$. A critic predicting $\hat Q(s,a_1)=1$ and $\hat Q(s,a_2)=10$ can fit observed targets while inducing a policy that selects $a_2$. This example illustrates extrapolation error; the tabular lower-bound derivations below require stronger coverage than this example provides. Offline RL and the conservative objective Offline RL learns from a fixed dataset $\mathcal D$ collected by a behavior policy $\pi_\beta$. Bellman targets query actions selected by the learned policy, although those actions may have little data support. Function approximation can overestimate their values; policy improvement then favors these actions and bootstrapping propagates the error. New interactions cannot correct it. CQL regularizes the critic rather than requiring an explicit behavior-policy model or constraint. For a policy $\pi_k$, write $y_k=r+\gamma\mathbb E_{a'\sim\pi_k(\cdot|s')}\hat Q^k(s',a')$ and $\mathcal L_{\rm TD}(Q)=\frac12\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}(Q(s,a)-y_k)^2$. Paper Eq. (1) adds $\alpha\mathbb E_{s\sim\mathcal D,a\sim\mu}Q(s,a)$, lowering values under a chosen action distribution $\mu$. Eq. (2) tightens this conservative estimate by also raising dataset-action values:
$$
\hat Q^{k+1}=\arg\min_Q\left{\mathcal L_{\rm TD}(Q)+\alpha\mathbb E_{s\sim\mathcal D}
\left[\mathbb E_{a\sim\mu(\cdot|s)}Q(s,a)-\mathbb E_{a\sim\hat\pi_\beta(\cdot|s)}Q(s,a)\right]\right}.
$$
Here $\hat\pi_\beta$ is empirical: its expectation is evaluated directly on dataset actions. The coefficient $\alpha$ balances Bellman fitting and conservatism. Expanding the entropy-regularized maximization The softmax calculation can also be written with an explicit temperature $\tau>0$. At a single state, solve $$
\max_{p\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\left{\sum_a p_a q_a-\tau\sum_a p_a\log p_a\right}.
$$ Introduce a multiplier $\nu$ for $\sum_a p_a=1$. Differentiating the Lagrangian with respect to each $p_a$ gives $$
q_a-\tau(\log p_a+1)-\nu=0,
\qquad
p_a=\exp\left(\frac{q_a-\nu}{\tau}-1\right).
$$ All actions share the same normalization factor, so $$
p_a^*=\frac{e^{q_a/\tau}}{\sum_b e^{q_b/\tau}},
\qquad
\max_p{p^\top q+\tau H(p)}=\tau\log\sum_a e^{q_a/\tau}.
$$ A useful check comes from the KL divergence. Defining $Z=\sum_a e^{q_a/\tau}$, $$
\tau D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p|p^*)
=\tau\sum_a p_a\log p_a-\sum_a p_aq_a+\tau\log Z.
$$ Rearranging shows that the objective equals $\tau\log Z-\tau D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p|p^ )$. Its maximum is attained at $p=p^ $ because KL divergence is nonnegative. Setting $\tau=1$ recovers CQL(H)'s log-sum-exp term. For numerical stability, compute it as $$
\tau\log\sum_a e^{q_a/\tau}
=m+\tau\log\sum_a e^{(q_a-m)/\tau},
\qquad m=\max_a q_a.
$$ Subtracting the maximum inside the exponential changes neither the value nor its gradient. It prevents large positive critic outputs from overflowing. What the regularizer changes With $R_s(Q)=\tau\log\sum_b e^{Q(s,b)/\tau}-\sum_b\beta(b|s)Q(s,b)$, $$
\frac{\partial R_s}{\partial Q(s,a)}
=\frac{e^{Q(s,a)/\tau}}{\sum_b e^{Q(s,b)/\tau}}-\beta(a|s).
$$ Gradient descent decreases an action's value when its softmax probability exceeds its dataset frequency. It increases that value when the inequality is reversed. The TD term still contributes its own gradient, so this sign calculation describes the conservative regularizer rather than the whole update. At a fixed state, adding a constant $c$ to every action value leaves $R_s$ unchanged: both terms increase by $c$. CQL(H) thus penalizes relative preferences over actions. The Bellman loss also remains necessary to anchor the absolute values. The implemented critic objective Substituting the entropy-regularized maximizer into the conservative objective gives CQL(H). With temperature one, its critic update is $$
\hat Q^{k+1}=\arg\min_Q\left{\mathcal L_{\rm TD}(Q)+\alpha\mathbb E_{s\sim\mathcal D}\left[\log\sum_a e^{Q(s,a)}-\mathbb E_{a\sim\hat\pi_\beta}Q(s,a)\right]\right}.
$$ The first term fits the Bellman target. The bracket compares the critic's soft maximum over actions with its value on dataset actions. CQL($\rho$) instead uses a reference distribution in the inner optimization; the original notes discuss a previous-policy prior as a way to reduce importance-weight variance. Discrete and continuous implementations For discrete actions, enumerate all actions, compute a stable log-sum-exp exactly, subtract the minibatch mean of $Q(s,a_{\rm data})$, and add the result to the TD loss. The paper builds its discrete variant on QR-DQN. For continuous actions, replace the sum by an integral. With proposal $q$ covering the action domain,
$$
\log\int e^{Q(s,a)},da\ \approx \operatorname{LSE} {i=1}^{N}\big[Q(s,a_i)-\log q(a_i)\big]-\log N,\qquad a_i\sim q.
$$
In the reference code's importance-sampled branch ($\mathtt{min_q_version}=3$), each transition supplies three groups: $a_u\sim U([-1,1]^d)$, $a_c\sim\pi \phi(\cdot|s)$, and $a_n\sim\pi_\phi(\cdot|s')$. All are evaluated at $s$. Concatenate $Q(s,a_u)-\log(2^{-d})$, $Q(s,a_c)-\log\pi_\phi(a_c|s)$, and $Q(s,a_n)-\log\pi_\phi(a_n|s')$, detaching policy log densities for the critic update. These are separate proposal corrections, not one mixture-density correction. The default temperature is one. The code takes their log-sum-exp, omits the constant $-\log(3N)$ for $N$ samples per group, subtracts mean data Q, and adds the weighted penalty to each critic's TD loss. This constant leaves critic gradients unchanged but shifts the threshold if the optional Lagrange multiplier is learned. The logarithm of a finite-sample integral estimate is generally biased. Expanding the continuous-action approximation For a bounded action domain $\mathcal A$, define the partition integral $$
Z_Q(s)=\int_{\mathcal A}e^{Q(s,a)/\tau},da.
$$ If a proposal density $q(a)$ is positive wherever the integrand contributes, multiply and divide by $q$: $$
Z_Q(s)=\mathbb E_{a\sim q}\left[\frac{e^{Q(s,a)/\tau}}{q(a)}\right].
$$ An unbiased estimate of $Z_Q$ is $\hat Z_Q=N^{-1}\sum_i e^{Q(s,a_i)/\tau}/q(a_i)$. Taking its logarithm gives $$
\tau\log\hat Z_Q
=\tau\operatorname{LSE}_i\left(\frac{Q(s,a_i)}{\tau}-\log q(a_i)\right)-\tau\log N.
$$ The density correction is inside the exponential's log argument. At temperature one this reduces to the expression above. Uniform sampling on $[-1,1]^d$ has density $2^{-d}$ because the box has volume $2^d$. If each of three proposals separately covers the integration domain and contributes $N$ samples, averaging their three importance estimates gives a $3N$-term estimator. This explains the constant $-\tau\log(3N)$. Alternatively, samples from a mixture can be corrected by the mixture density; that is a different estimator. A proposal that misses part of the support does not become a valid full-domain importance estimator just because its log density is subtracted. For fixed $\alpha$, omitting $-\tau\log(3N)$ adds a constant to the critic loss, so the critic gradient is unchanged. If $\alpha$ is optimized against a target action gap, the multiplier sees the shifted numerical gap. Sample count, temperature and the chosen threshold then need to be considered together. Finally, unbiasedness of $\hat Z_Q$ does not imply unbiasedness of $\log\hat Z_Q$. Jensen's inequality gives $$
\mathbb E[\log\hat Z_Q]\leq\log\mathbb E[\hat Z_Q]=\log Z_Q.
$$ This sampling effect is separate from the conservatism introduced by the objective. Finite-action enumeration avoids this particular integration approximation. Deriving the tabular lower bound Hold the Bellman target $y(s,a)$ fixed during one critic update. At one state, the part of Eq. (2) depending on its action values is $$
J_s(Q)=\frac12\sum_a\beta(a|s)[Q(s,a)-y(s,a)]^2
+\alpha\sum_a[\mu(a|s)-\beta(a|s)]Q(s,a).
$$ The state marginal multiplies both terms and cancels from the first-order condition. For each covered action, $$
\frac{\partial J_s}{\partial Q(s,a)}
=\beta(a|s)[Q(s,a)-y(s,a)]
+\alpha[\mu(a|s)-\beta(a|s)]=0.
$$ Dividing by $\beta(a|s)$ yields $$
Q_{\mathrm{new}}(s,a)=y(s,a)-\alpha\left(\frac{\mu(a|s)}{\beta(a|s)}-1\right).
$$ This division is precisely where the coverage assumption enters. It is undefined for an unseen action with zero empirical probability; a neural network's extrapolation to that action cannot be justified by this calculation alone. For policy evaluation, take $\mu=\pi$ and define $c(s,a)=\pi(a|s)/\beta(a|s)-1$. Under an exact Bellman operator, the fixed point satisfies $$
\hat Q^\pi=r+\gamma P^\pi\hat Q^\pi-\alpha c,
\qquad
Q^\pi=r+\gamma P^\pi Q^\pi.
$$ Here $(P^\pi Q)(s,a)=\sum_{s'}P(s'|s,a)\sum_{a'}\pi(a'|s')Q(s',a')$. Subtracting gives $$
Q^\pi-\hat Q^\pi=\alpha(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}c
=\alpha\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t(P^\pi)^t c.
$$ The series converges because $\gamma<1$. However, $c(s,a)$ can be negative. This expression does not establish a pointwise lower bound on $\hat Q^\pi$. To obtain the policy-value statement, average the penalty over the same policy: $$
\bar c(s)=\sum_a\pi(a|s)c(s,a)
=\sum_a\frac{\pi(a|s)^2}{\beta(a|s)}-1
=\sum_a\frac{[\pi(a|s)-\beta(a|s)]^2}{\beta(a|s)}\geq0.
$$ The last equality follows by expanding the square and using that both distributions sum to one. This is a Pearson $\chi^2$ divergence. It vanishes when $\pi=\beta$ and grows when the evaluated policy assigns probability to actions rare in the dataset. Let $P_\pi(s'|s)=\sum_a\pi(a|s)P(s'|s,a)$ and $\hat V^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a|s)\hat Q^\pi(s,a)$. Averaging the fixed-point equations gives $$
V^\pi-\hat V^\pi
=\gamma P_\pi(V^\pi-\hat V^\pi)+\alpha\bar c,
$$ hence $$
V^\pi-\hat V^\pi
=\alpha(I-\gamma P_\pi)^{-1}\bar c
=\alpha\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^tP_\pi^t\bar c\geq0.
$$ Every transition probability and every entry of $\bar c$ is nonnegative. This proves the expected-value lower bound in the exact, covered, tabular setting. For Eq. (1), the same differentiation instead produces a penalty $\alpha\mu(a|s)/\beta(a|s)$, which is nonnegative action by action. That stronger penalty explains the pointwise bound and its greater pessimism. A one-state check Take a one-state MDP with $\gamma=0$, $\beta=(1/2,1/2)$ and $\pi=(3/4,1/4)$. Eq. (2) gives $c=(1/2,-1/2)$, so $$
\hat Q(a_1)=r(a_1)-\alpha/2,
\qquad
\hat Q(a_2)=r(a_2)+\alpha/2.
$$ The second action's estimate exceeds its true value. Yet $$
V^\pi-\hat V^\pi
=\alpha[(3/4)(1/2)+(1/4)(-1/2)]=\alpha/4\geq0.
$$ This is an explicit example of a conservative policy value without conservative values for every action. What sampling error changes With an empirical operator, write $e=(\hat{\mathcal B}^\pi-\mathcal B^\pi)\hat Q$. The fixed-point subtraction becomes $$
Q^\pi-\hat Q=(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}(\alpha c-e).
$$ In state-value form, if $\bar e(s)=\mathbb E_{a\sim\pi}e(s,a)$, a sufficient condition for the same nonnegative propagation argument is $\alpha\bar c(s)\geq\bar e(s)$ at every evaluated state. This is a sufficient condition for this derivation, not a replacement for the paper's finite-sample theorem. Concentration bounds control $e$ probabilistically. If $\bar c(s)=0$, increasing $\alpha$ cannot directly create a margin at that state through this particular penalty. Assumptions and lower-bound theorems The basic analysis assumes a discounted MDP ($0\leq\gamma<1$), bounded rewards, dataset-state evaluation, sufficient action coverage, and exactly represented/solved Q-iterations. In particular, $\operatorname{supp}\mu\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\hat\pi_\beta$; the paper simplifies the derivation by assuming positive empirical behavior probabilities for all actions at dataset states. Empirical reward/transition errors obey high-probability concentration bounds that decrease with sample counts. The conservative coefficient must be large enough to dominate their propagated error. Sparse coverage weakens the guarantee; extensions to linear approximation and neural tangent kernels require further assumptions. Theorem 3.1 concerns the fixed point of Eq. (1): sufficiently large $\alpha$ gives a pointwise lower bound $\hat Q^\pi(s,a)\leq Q^\pi(s,a)$ on the stated domain. Theorem 3.2 concerns Eq. (2) with $\mu=\pi$: the tighter guarantee is $\hat V^\pi(s)=\mathbb E_\pi\hat Q^\pi(s,a)\leq V^\pi(s)$, and need not hold for each action. The underlying tabular update illustrates why:
$$
\hat Q^{k+1}=\hat{\mathcal B}^{\pi}\hat Q^k-\alpha\left(\frac{\pi}{\hat\pi_\beta}-1\right),
\qquad
\mathbb E_\pi\left[\frac{\pi}{\hat\pi_\beta}-1\right]
=\sum_a\frac{\pi(a|s)^2}{\hat\pi_\beta(a|s)}-1\geq0.
$$
The nonnegative expected penalty propagates through Bellman evaluation. With an exact Bellman operator, any positive $\alpha$ suffices for these evaluation bounds; finite-sample error requires a sufficient margin. Bounds can also hold during Q-iteration: Theorem 3.3 requires the improved policy to remain close in total variation to $\pi_{\hat Q^k}\propto e^{\hat Q^k}$. Writing that distance as at most $\epsilon$, a sufficient condition in the exact-operator setting is
$$
\mathbb E_{a\sim\pi_{\hat Q^k}}\left[\frac{\pi_{\hat Q^k}(a|s)}{\hat\pi_\beta(a|s)}-1\right]
\geq\epsilon\max_{a:\hat\pi_\beta(a|s)>0}\frac{\pi_{\hat Q^k}(a|s)}{\hat\pi_\beta(a|s)}.
$$
Thus conservatism must outweigh policy mismatch. These are conditional guarantees for theoretical Q-iterations, not every neural-network gradient step. Theorem 3.4 formalizes expansion of the expected gap between data and penalized actions. Theorems 3.5-3.6 characterize a behavior-divergence-penalized empirical return and high-probability safe improvement, with slack depending on sampling error and distribution shift. Learning or computing a policy The continuous actor minimizes a SAC-style objective $\mathbb E_{s\sim\mathcal D,a\sim\pi_\phi}[\lambda\log\pi_\phi(a|s)-\min_jQ_{\theta_j}(s,a)]$, using reparameterized gradients with fixed critic parameters. Here $\lambda$ is the actor entropy temperature, distinct from the conservative coefficient $\alpha$; actor and critic updates alternate. Alternatively, discrete actions permit a greedy policy $\arg\max_a Q(s,a)$ or the entropy-regularized solution $\pi_Q(a|s)=e^{Q(s,a)/\lambda}/\sum_b e^{Q(s,b)/\lambda}$. Continuous actions permit numerical maximization of $Q(s,a)$ at each state, or sampling from its normalized Boltzmann density, at extra computational cost. Experimental results and baseline comparisons The paper's D4RL results use normalized returns averaged over four seeds. On walker2d-medium-expert, CQL(H) scores 98.7 versus BC 11.3, BEAR 10.8, offline SAC 1.9, and BRAC-v 0.9 (Table 1), supporting its usefulness on mixed behavior data. On antmaze-medium-play it reaches 61.2 while all listed baselines score zero (Table 2), suggesting useful recombination of suboptimal trajectories. Improvements are not universal: halfcheetah-expert scores 104.8 versus BEAR 108.2 and BC 107.0; pen-cloned also favors BC. CQL($\rho$) can be more stable on high-dimensional Adroit tasks. The discrete Atari results support data efficiency: with 1% of replay data, Breakout returns are 61.1 for CQL, 11.0 for REM, and 7.9 for QR-DQN (Table 3). Table 4 tests conservatism directly: hopper-medium's predicted-minus-true value is -7.48 for CQL(H), versus -156.70 for Eq. (1) and +4.32 for BEAR. This supports a tighter conservative estimate, while remaining empirical evidence on selected tasks rather than an unconditional neural-network guarantee. Reading the objective in practice The coefficient $\alpha$ controls a tradeoff: too little conservatism can leave unsupported actions attractive, while too much can suppress useful policy improvement. A low critic loss alone cannot resolve that tradeoff. Coverage, the policy update, the action proposals and the target construction all affect what the learned values mean. The tabular derivation gives a precise reason for the lower bound: the policy-averaged penalty is nonnegative and the discounted transition operator propagates it with nonnegative weights. The neural implementation retains the objective's structure, but exact minimization, full coverage and exact Bellman evaluation are no longer available. Its training curves therefore need to be interpreted as empirical behavior under those approximations. References [1] A. Kumar, A. Zhou, G. Tucker, and S. Levine. Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning. NeurIPS 2020. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04779v3 [2] Authors' reference implementation, CQLTrainer. https://github.com/aviralkumar2907/CQL/blob/master/d4rl/rlkit/torch/sac/cql.py

1 - Introduction to UVM
description: The Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) is a standardized and widely used framework for functional verification of complex designs. It enables constrained random, coverage-driven verification and provides the tools to create configurable and flexible testbenches. UVM helps engineers focus on verifying IP blocks and encourages reuse across projects.
body:
The Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) is a standardized and widely used framework for functional verification of complex designs. It enables constrained random, coverage-driven verification and provides the tools to create  configurable  and  flexible testbenches . UVM helps engineers focus on verifying IP blocks and encourages reuse across projects. Key Features of UVM Constrained Random Coverage-Driven Verification Separation of Tests from Testbenches Transaction-Level Communication Layered Sequential Stimulus Standardized Messaging Register Layers Emphasis on Reuse Why Reuse is Key Reusing components, sequences, and testbenches reduces effort and ensures consistency across verification projects. This principle drives the modular design of UVM. Constrained Random verification Constrained random verification combines the unpredictability of random inputs with constraints to ensure legal and valid scenarios. This methodology uncovers unexpected behaviors, enabling engineers to: Identify whether behaviors are bugs or features. Uncover scenarios that might not have been considered. Automate stimulus generation. Random input lead to random output, which means we don't know what the output are. Therefore we need to implement a checker. The checker can be reference model. Ensure we test everything. We start we a verification plan. From this, we develop a function coverage model. This can be a set of checks, assertions or anything's. We need to track this to ensure all of the randomness test everything we need to cover. For example did we test all the transition of the state machine, test all the aspect of the protocol. UVM allow you use the constrained random environment to uncover the thing you haven't thought about. Once you thought about this, then you can modify the constraints. It allow use to increase our coverage and target more aspect in our verification plans. Test vs Testbench Testbench Defines the  verification environment  that interacts with the Design Under Test (DUT). It includes all components like drivers, monitors, and scoreboards, ensuring: High configurability Reusability across multiple tests Test Specifies the exact configurations and sequences for a particular simulation run. Tests define: Values and parameters Implementations Specific sequences to run

Tests define: Values and parameters Implementations Specific sequences to run By separating tests from the testbench, UVM allows easy modification of scenarios without altering the core environment. Layered Sequential Stimulus Stimulus  is to drive the transaction into the DUT.
 Transaction  is encapsulation of any information we need to communicate to the DUT. For bus, transaction can be address and data. It is kind of like Struct in C.
The  transaction  send to the  driver .
The driver turn transaction to digital signal to the DUT.
A sequence is a specification of a chain of transactions. The sequence can be reactive chain which the transaction can based on previous transaction's output.
It can also be layered so you can have sequence of sequence. We called  virtual sequence . It coordinate the operation of other sequence and those sequence can run in parallel or sequentially. It can create as complex a set of scenarios as you need. The Big Picture Verification Components Agent : Encapsulates key components like sequencer, driver, and monitor. Sequencer : Generates sequences and communicates with the driver. Driver : Converts sequences to pin-level signals for the DUT. Monitor : Observes pin-level activity and translates it back into transactions. Environment Components Scoreboards : Validate outputs. Coverage Collectors : Track coverage metrics. Analysis Components : Perform deeper validation. Coordination Virtual Sequence : Orchestrates activities across components. Configuration Database : Allows tests to modify and configure the verification environment dynamically. With UVM, multiple tests can be created and organized into a library. This structure promotes reuse and consistency. What is next

title: ELEC 402 VLSI System Summary
description: A connected review of CMOS capacitance, logical effort, logic families, power and sequential timing, with worked equations alongside the original figures.
body:
A CMOS design has to produce the right logic levels within a timing budget and a power budget. These constraints interact: a wider transistor can drive a load faster, but it also loads the preceding stage and consumes more switching energy. The useful question is usually which part of the path limits the design, and what changes when that part is resized. MOS capacitance and the load seen by a gate A gate's load includes the inputs it drives, the interconnect, and capacitance at its own output node: $$
C_L=C_{\mathrm{fanout}}+C_{\mathrm{wire}}+C_{\mathrm{self}}.
$$ The fanout term comes from the next gates' input capacitances. The self-loading term includes drain diffusion and other output-node parasitics. Keeping them separate helps avoid counting the same physical contribution twice. For a long-channel device, the intrinsic oxide capacitance scales approximately as $C_{ox}WL$. How that capacitance is distributed among terminals depends on the operating region. In the ideal saturation model, the channel contribution to $C_{gs}$ is approximately $\frac23 C_{ox}WL$ and the intrinsic $C_{gd}$ is approximately zero. Physical overlap capacitance remains, so an intrinsic-channel formula cannot be used as the complete device capacitance. When using a width-normalized capacitance such as $\bar C_g$, check its units first. If $\bar C_g$ is capacitance per unit width and length is fixed, an input driven by both NMOS and PMOS gates has approximately $$
C_{in}=\bar C_g(W_n+W_p).
$$ This equation is also the conversion from a capacitance target back to transistor widths. A capacitance is a load specification; it is not itself a width. Combinational delay and logical effort Start with the capacitances Sizing begins by identifying everything connected to the node being driven. Fanout count alone is insufficient: four small gate inputs can present a different load from four large ones. Wire capacitance also remains even if the receiving gate is resized. A first-order delay model is $t\approx R_{eq}C_L$. Increasing device width reduces effective resistance roughly inversely with width, while increasing input and diffusion capacitance roughly in proportion to width. Enlarging every transistor therefore does not make a path arbitrarily fast. Each gate becomes a heavier load for its predecessor. Normalize delay before comparing gates Logical effort separates normalized stage delay into an effort term and a parasitic term: $$
d=gh+p,\qquad h=\frac{C_{out}}{C_{in}},\qquad t=\tau d.
$$ Here $g$ compares the gate's input capacitance with that of an inverter having the same output drive, $h$ is electrical effort, and $p$ is parasitic delay. The technology-dependent $\tau$ converts normalized delay to time. Course notes may express $p$ using a separate parasitic ratio; that convention must be checked before substituting values. An inverter has $g=1$ by definition. A complex gate's logical effort is input dependent: match its drive resistance to the reference inverter, then compare the capacitance presented at the input being analyzed. Series stacks usually require larger transistors to retain the reference drive strength. Balance the effort across a path For $N$ stages, define logical effort $G=\prod_i g_i$, electrical effort $H=C_{load}/C_{in,1}$, and branching effort $B=\prod_i b_i$. At a branch, $$
b_i=\frac{C_{\mathrm{on\ path}}+C_{\mathrm{off\ path}}}{C_{\mathrm{on\ path}}}.
$$ The off-path loads still have to be charged. Ignoring them makes the chosen path appear faster than it is. With consistent load accounting, the path effort is $F=GBH=\prod_i f_i$, where $f_i=g_i b_i h_i$ when $h_i$ counts the on-path load. For fixed stage count and approximately fixed parasitics, $$
D=\sum_{i=1}^N f_i+P\geq N F^{1/N}+P,
\qquad P=\sum_i p_i.
$$ The arithmetic-geometric mean inequality gives the minimum when all stage efforts are equal: $f_i=F^{1/N}$. After choosing $N$, work backward from the final load to find each input capacitance. In the unbranched case, $$
C_{in,i}=\frac{g_i C_{out,i}}{f_i}.
$$ For a fixed PMOS-to-NMOS width ratio $r=W_p/W_n$, the corresponding widths are $W_n=C_{in}/[\bar C_g(1+r)]$ and $W_p=rW_n$. The ratio comes from the chosen drive model, not from logical effort alone. For an inverter-only path with no parasitic delay, $D(N)=NH^{1/N}$. Treating $N$ as continuous gives a best stage effort of $e$. Including parasitics generally shifts the preferred effort upward; a value around four is a practical starting point, not a universal optimum. Compare nearby integer stage counts and preserve the required output polarity. The sizing procedure is therefore: determine the path and its branches, compute $F$, compare feasible stage counts, balance the stage efforts, and convert the resulting capacitances into widths. Layout-dependent wire loads and input slew can require another iteration. Pseudo-NMOS logic Pseudo-NMOS uses an always-on PMOS pull-up and an NMOS pull-down network. With the pull-down off, the output approaches $V_{DD}$. With the pull-down on, both networks conduct. The low output voltage is set by their current balance, so this is ratioed logic. At the desired low level, solve $$
I_n(V_{OL})=|I_p(V_{OL})|.
$$ Under a long-channel approximation with the NMOS in its linear region and the PMOS saturated, $$
\beta_n\left[(V_{DD}-V_{Tn})V_{OL}-\frac{V_{OL}^2}{2}\right]
\approx\frac{\beta_p}{2}(V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|)^2.
$$ The device-region assumptions must hold for the chosen voltages. A stronger PMOS improves pull-up speed but increases contention and typically raises $V_{OL}$. A weaker PMOS makes it easier to pull the output low but slows the rising transition. The low-output state dissipates static power approximately equal to $V_{DD}I_{\mathrm{contention}}$. Reducing the device count can save area and input capacitance, but it does not remove the cost of a continuous current path. Noise margins, rise time and static power must be checked together. Dynamic logic Precharge and evaluation A dynamic gate stores a voltage on a capacitive node. In the usual NMOS evaluation topology, precharge connects that node to $V_{DD}$. During evaluation, the precharge transistor turns off and the pull-down network may discharge the node. If it does not discharge, the high value must survive until it is sampled. A clocked footer can isolate the pull-down path during precharge. Device-count comparisons depend on the topology: an NMOS network with $N$ transistors plus a precharge transistor and a footer uses $N+2$ devices before any output inverter or keeper is counted. That count is not a formula for every Boolean function or dynamic gate. Why monotonicity matters During evaluation, a discharged dynamic node cannot be restored by the precharge transistor. For an NMOS pull-down gate, inputs should therefore remain stable or transition from zero to one during that phase. A one-to-zero transition can leave the node discharged even though the final input combination should not discharge it. The dynamic output can fall during evaluation. Driving another NMOS dynamic stage directly can consequently violate the next stage's input requirement. An intervening static inverter turns that falling dynamic output into a rising signal. This dynamic/static combination is a domino stage. Its straightforward cascades implement non-inverting logic between stage boundaries. Zipper logic alternates suitable NMOS and PMOS dynamic stages. The polarity and permitted transition direction must be checked at every boundary; alternating transistor types alone does not establish correct timing. Charge sharing, leakage and clock coupling Charge sharing occurs when a precharged output connects to initially uncharged internal capacitances. Ignoring leakage, threshold effects and other paths, conservation of charge gives $$
C_LV_{DD}=(C_L+C_X)V_{\mathrm{final}},
\qquad
V_{\mathrm{final}}=V_{DD}\frac{C_L}{C_L+C_X}.
$$ The output can fall even without a complete path to ground. The relevant test is whether it stays above the receiving gate's switching threshold with sufficient noise margin. Internal-node precharge and circuit restructuring can help, with additional capacitance and clock load as costs. Leakage gradually changes the stored voltage. For an approximately constant leakage current over an evaluation interval, $$
\Delta V\approx\frac{I_{leak}\Delta t}{C_L}.
$$ A keeper supplies a weak restoring current, but it can oppose a legitimate discharge. Keeper sizing is another contention-versus-retention tradeoff. A larger dynamic capacitance reduces voltage disturbance for a given lost charge, while requiring more energy and discharge current. Clock feed-through is capacitive coupling from the clock into the dynamic node, including through the precharge device. Dynamic-gate reliability consequently depends on the clock waveform, the evaluation interval, internal-node charge and input transitions. A static truth table does not capture these conditions. Power and energy Separate energy per operation from power Instantaneous power is $p(t)=v(t)i(t)$, energy is $E=\int p(t),dt$, and average power is $E/T$. A lower average power can simply mean fewer operations per second. Energy per operation is the more useful comparison when the designs have different throughput. Charging a capacitance from zero to $V_{DD}$ draws charge $CV_{DD}$ from the supply, so the supply delivers $CV_{DD}^2$. Half is stored on the capacitor; the rest is dissipated in the charging path. Discharging dissipates the stored half. A complete charge/discharge cycle therefore dissipates $CV_{DD}^2$ in the ideal capacitive model. If $\alpha_{01}$ is the expected number of zero-to-one charging events per clock cycle, $$
P_{\mathrm{switch}}=\alpha_{01}CV_{DD}^2f.
$$ Some texts instead define activity as the number of transitions in either direction and include a factor of one half. Always identify which events the activity factor counts. Activity and clock gating For independent values in consecutive cycles with probability $p$ of a logic one, $\alpha_{01}=(1-p)p$. Temporal correlation changes that result. Combinational glitches can also add charging events beyond what a cycle-boundary Boolean probability predicts. Clock gating reduces clock transitions in unused sequential blocks. It can also reduce switching driven by those registers, but it does not eliminate switching caused by unrelated changing inputs, nor does it eliminate leakage. The clock-enable signal must be generated safely so that the gated clock does not acquire short pulses. Capacitance, voltage and frequency Smaller gates and shorter wires reduce switched capacitance. Their timing effects differ: shrinking a gate lowers its input load while weakening its drive. Floorplanning can reduce a wire's load without relying on that same drive tradeoff. Lowering voltage has a quadratic effect in the capacitive power model, but also reduces drive current and increases delay. Select voltage and frequency together under the required workload and timing constraints. Crossing voltage domains may require level conversion, especially when a low-voltage output cannot meet a high-voltage input's required logic-high level. PDP and EDP Using the same operation boundary and defining average power over its execution time $D$, its energy is $E=P_{avg}D$. Under that convention, the power-delay product equals energy, while the energy-delay product is $EDP=ED=P_{avg}D^2$. The convention matters. Multiplying a measured long-term average power by an unrelated single-gate propagation delay does not automatically give energy per useful operation. Likewise, reducing voltage cannot reduce energy without limit: leakage, longer runtime and functional voltage limits eventually matter. Short-circuit and static power During an input transition, both NMOS and PMOS devices can conduct simultaneously. The short-circuit energy is approximately $$
E_{sc}=V_{DD}\int I_{sc}(t),dt.
$$ Slow input edges can lengthen this overlap. The output load also affects the device voltages during the transition, so short-circuit current should be analyzed with the input slew and load together. A fast edge is not free if producing it requires a much larger upstream driver. Static power includes subthreshold, junction and gate leakage, with contributions depending on process and bias conditions. It also includes sustained contention in ratioed circuits. Unlike the capacitive switching term, these currents can persist when the clock stops. A useful power estimate separates switching, short-circuit and leakage contributions before choosing an optimization. Clock gating addresses activity; resizing changes capacitance and drive; supply scaling changes both energy and achievable speed. The largest term in the measured workload determines which change is worth making. Sequential circuits and timing closure A latch is transparent during one clock level. An edge-triggered flip-flop samples around a clock edge. Both require data to remain stable over a setup/hold interval; the distinction changes how time can be allocated between stages. Let $t_{cq}$ be launch clock-to-Q delay, $t_{comb}$ the combinational delay, and $t_{setup}$ the capture setup requirement. With zero skew and no additional uncertainty, $$
T_{clk}\geq t_{cq,\max}+t_{comb,\max}+t_{setup}.
$$ Define clock skew as $t_{skew}=t_{capture}-t_{launch}$. A positive value means the capture clock arrives later. The corresponding setup and hold checks are $$
T_{clk}\geq t_{cq,\max}+t_{comb,\max}+t_{setup}-t_{skew},
$$ $$
t_{cq,\min}+t_{comb,\min}\geq t_{hold}+t_{skew}.
$$ Positive skew helps setup but makes hold harder under this convention. Setup constrains the longest path; hold constrains the shortest path. Reducing clock frequency can help setup, but it does not repair a same-edge hold violation. Practical checks also include jitter, clock uncertainty and variation margins. For latch-based designs, transparency permits time borrowing, but the analysis must include the latch opening and closing times and the following stage's budget. Borrowed time is taken from another part of the path. What to carry into a design problem Begin with the required function and legal signal transitions. Identify the physical loads, estimate delay, and size the path against its timing constraint. Then evaluate switching activity and energy using the actual workload. Dynamic and ratioed logic add retention or contention checks that static CMOS timing alone cannot supply. The recurring constraint is that an improvement at one node changes the work done elsewhere: a larger gate loads its predecessor, a keeper opposes discharge, and a slower low-voltage path spends longer leaking. The final circuit has to satisfy logic levels, setup and hold, and power limits at the same time. For further worked examples, see  David Harris’s CMOS VLSI lectures .
